title: A heavy leg with preserved automatic strength

blocks.text: A heavy leg with preserved automatic strength

AMaC MRCP PACES · R5-171 · Neurological examination · PACES Station 3, neurological examination · Skills A, B, D, E, G · 10 minutes (up to 6 examination, at least 4 questions) · Guideline dates and links in section 15 · Related AMaC: condition may appear elsewhere in a different context

Dear Doctor, examine the lower limbs of a woman aged 29, whose right leg feels weak. Symptoms have been stable for four months after an initial hospital assessment. Assess the pattern and discuss your interpretation. Please obtain consent before demonstrating any additional manoeuvre. Do not test walking without first checking safety.

sections.heading: 4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap

blocks.text: HOOK: Compare voluntary movement with automatic movement using a correctly performed Hoover manoeuvre.
TRAP: A normal scan does not diagnose functional weakness; a positive sign is supportive clinical evidence, not proof of deception or exclusion of every other disorder.

rows: “I will check strength, reflexes and sensation before explaining the pattern.”
Assess tone, power, reflexes and plantar responses with consistent instructions.
“Push this heel down; now lift the other leg against my hand.”
Compare weak voluntary right hip extension with the right heel’s automatic downward pressure during resisted left hip flexion.
“Your leg produces more strength automatically than when you try directly.”
Describe the observation as evidence that movement pathways can function; avoid confrontation.
Keep the diagnosis open to coexisting disease.
“These symptoms are real, and new symptoms still deserve assessment.”
Seek a positive specialist diagnosis and plan function-focused rehabilitation with a safety net.
Examines safely in the bed first.
Agrees a stop signal and uses assistance for standing if needed.
Finds normal tone, symmetrical reflexes and flexor plantars.
Reports the positive movement discrepancy rather than relying on normal findings.
Uses the wrong leg or no resistance.
Demonstrates increased right hip extension during resisted left hip flexion.
Checks comprehension and pain, and repeats once to establish reproducibility.
Considers functional leg weakness from the positive pattern.
Explains the sign’s limits and retains a route for neurological comorbidity.
Discharges without an explanation or plan.
Suggests specialist confirmation and tailored rehabilitation.
Sets an achievable functional goal and coordinates care rather than ordering repeated untargeted scans.
Uses surprise or humiliation to catch the patient out.
Describes symptoms as genuine and avoids blame.
Checks how the explanation lands and provides a specific response to new neurological red flags.

blocks.text: High-performance is an AMaC teaching label, not an official grade.
Skills: A physical examination; B identifying physical signs; C clinical communication; D differential diagnosis; E clinical judgement; F managing patients’ concerns; G maintaining patient welfare.

Patient: a nursery worker, off work because the right leg feels heavy. The onset was gradual over several days after back discomfort; the original hospital assessment included brain and spinal imaging without a structural explanation. The discomfort has resolved. You still need a stick outdoors and have good and bad days. No new bladder retention, saddle numbness, severe back pain or progressive loss of function now.

Your concern is that “functional” will mean invented. If asked about mood, say that disability has made you anxious; do not provide a hidden trauma story to explain the diagnosis. Medicines: occasional paracetamol; no regular sedatives or allergies. Opening: “I know the scan was normal, but the leg is not.” If the candidate explains a sign respectfully, you ask whether rehabilitation can help. If accused of poor effort, become upset. A trained role-player or examiner-described findings must be used consistently; the patient is not instructed to manufacture an unexplained neurological deficit during an unbriefed examination.

Findings and delivery. Lower-limb bulk and tone are normal; reflexes are symmetrical and plantar responses flexor. Direct right hip extension appears weak. When the candidate asks the patient to flex the left hip against resistance while feeling under the right heel, right hip extension becomes clearly stronger. The difference is reproducible after checking instructions and absence of pain. Other right-leg power varies across tasks without a coherent pyramidal distribution. No definite sensory level is supplied. If safely assessed, supported standing shows better weight bearing than expected from direct bed testing. Do not invent a precise MRC grade for every inconsistent effort or claim that the manoeuvre alone establishes all aspects of the diagnosis.

Question ladder. Q1 (R3) Explain Hoover’s sign. Weak voluntary hip extension becomes stronger during contralateral resisted hip flexion, demonstrating a discrepancy between voluntary and automatic activation. Q2 (R4) What can interfere with interpretation? Pain, misunderstanding, attention and other neurological problems may affect testing; interpret within the whole examination. Q3 (R4) Why not diagnose from the scan? Functional neurological disorder is supported by positive clinical features. Normal imaging alone is insufficient and some organic disease may coexist. Q4 (R5) How would you explain it? Describe a genuine problem with movement control and demonstrate preserved function with permission. Avoid saying it is imaginary or simply caused by stress. Q5 (R6) When would you reassess urgently? New sudden weakness, sphincter dysfunction, saddle sensory loss, major back pain or other acute neurological signs require appropriate emergency assessment.
Performs the correct contralateral manoeuvre (A).
Describes improved automatic extension accurately (B).
Gives a positive, non-accusatory interpretation (D G).
Supports rehabilitation while preserving a pathway for new disease (E).
Fail performance
CANDIDATE: “The MRI is normal, so nothing is wrong.” [R4 Fail] Pushes both heels down without contralateral resistance, then says the patient is not trying. [R3 Fail R6 Fail]
Pass performance

CANDIDATE demonstrates the voluntary/automatic discrepancy and considers functional weakness within a complete neurological assessment. [R2 Pass R3 Pass R4 Pass] “This is a real movement-control problem for which rehabilitation may help.” [R5 Pass R6 Pass]
High-performance performance

CANDIDATE checks pain and understanding, shows the preserved movement with permission and asks what the patient understands by the explanation. [R3 High R6 High] A return-to-work goal is paired with specialist rehabilitation and a clear safety net. [R5 High] EXAMINER: diagnoses constructively without treating a single sign as infallible.
R3: Reversing the legs or omitting resistance demonstrates no interpretable Hoover sign.
R4: A positive functional sign does not prove deliberate symptom production.
R5: Reassurance without rehabilitation leaves the disability unaddressed.
“I have described the scan, but I should explain the positive examination finding.”
“Let me check this movement is comfortable and my instructions were clear.”
“I believe the symptoms; the sign tells us something useful about movement control.”

Hoover’s sign compares voluntary hip extension with involuntary extension during resisted opposite hip flexion. The finding supports functional weakness in the appropriate clinical context; it is not a lie detector. Diagnosis and explanation usually require a clinician experienced in neurological assessment. Symptoms can fluctuate, and new features should not automatically be attributed to an established functional diagnosis. Rehabilitation can focus on retraining movement and meaningful activities; psychological support may help some patients without being a compulsory explanation for all.
THINK: Positive discrepancy, not merely negative scans.
SAY: “The automatic movement shows that useful strength is available.”
DO: Correct heel comparison; check pain and understanding.
NUMBERS: No sensitivity or specificity figure is needed.
TRAP: Calling symptoms deliberate.
FINISH: Clear explanation, specialist plan and functional goals.
